title: The open redirect
context: A developer asked an AI assistant to redirect users back to the page they came from after logging in, using a 'next' query parameter. The suggested code works for normal navigation, but it also lets attackers craft login links that silently send victims to a phishing site right after they authenticate.
question: What's the risk in a link like /login/callback?next=https://evil-lookalike.com/login ?
options: Open redirect — redirectTo comes straight from an unvalidated query parameter, so an attacker can send a legitimate login link that redirects victims to a phishing site right after they authenticate.
authenticateUser runs after the redirect, so the user is never actually logged in.
req.query.next is undefined unless the request uses POST instead of GET.
res.redirect only accepts relative paths, so the external URL is ignored automatically.

explanation.theBug: redirectTo is taken directly from a user-controlled query parameter with no validation that it points somewhere on the app's own domain. Because the link comes from the real login flow, it looks completely legitimate — the victim really does log in — but lands them on an attacker-controlled page immediately afterward, a proven and commonly-exploited phishing technique called an open redirect.
explanation.whyAIGeneratesThis: Redirecting back to where the user came from is a genuinely common and reasonable feature request, and reading the destination from a query parameter is the obvious way to implement it. The model treats req.query.next as ordinary application data rather than untrusted input that needs to be constrained to the app's own domain — that threat model isn't implied by the feature description alone.

theFix.commentary: Only allow redirect targets that match a strict relative-path pattern — never redirect to a value that could contain a protocol or host, even one that looks like your own domain.

explanation.reviewHeuristic: Any redirect target sourced from a query parameter or form field must be validated against an allowlist of relative paths — never trust it to already point somewhere safe.
